title: Why fluids produce upthrust
prior_knowledge_summary: Hydrostatic pressure difference in a uniform static fluid is found from Δp = ρgΔh.
Pressure difference depends on vertical depth difference, not on the absolute depth values separately.
Pressure acting normally on an area produces a force, and forces have direction.
new_learning: Explain upthrust as the upward resultant of pressure forces on an immersed object.
Explain why the deeper lower surface experiences a larger pressure force than the upper surface.
Recognise when horizontal pressure-force components cancel.
not_yet_taught: Calculating upthrust from fluid density and displaced volume

visual_planning.deferral_reason: This bounded delivery contains the four JSON files only; figure briefs are ready for a later visual-production pass.
visual_planning.style: Landscape rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketches with sparse labels and purposeful colour.

blocks.heading: Why does the water push the block upward?
content: Hold a sealed plastic block below the surface of a still tank and let go. Before thinking about whether it eventually rises or sinks, focus on one question: can the water itself produce an upward force on the block?
Water presses on every face. That can sound as if all the pushes should cancel. Predict which face receives the larger pressure force, the top or the bottom, and explain what depth has to do with it.
The answer will come from two ideas already known: pressure changes with depth, and pressure produces a force normal to a surface.

figure.purpose: Create a prediction puzzle about the resultant of fluid pressure forces.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper teacher sketch of a small rectangular block held fully below calm water. Show short inward pressure arrows around all faces, but do not yet label an upthrust arrow or identify which force is larger. Mark top and bottom depths with simple brackets.
figure.alt_text: A submerged block has inward water-pressure arrows on every face and marked top and bottom depths.

blocks.heading: Pressure pushes normally
content: At each point on the block, the fluid force is perpendicular to the surface. On the top face it acts downward. On the bottom face it acts upward. On the vertical faces it acts horizontally.
The formula to remember is p = F/A. For a flat face at one depth, rearrange it as F = pA. Here p is pressure in pascals, F is the normal force in newtons and A is area in square metres.
Imagine the water replaced by many tiny hands that always push straight into the block. The hands show direction. The pressure at their depth tells us how strong their combined push is.

symbols: p is pressure in pascals, Pa.
F is the normal force in newtons, N.
A is the area in square metres, m².
formula_to_remember.units: Pressure is in Pa, force in N and area in m².

figure.purpose: Connect surface orientation to the direction of each pressure force.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper annotated sketch of a submerged cuboid. Use black outlines and coloured arrows perpendicular to each face. Label top force downward, bottom force upward and paired side forces horizontal. Add a small F = pA reminder without comparing magnitudes yet.
figure.alt_text: Pressure forces act perpendicular to the top, bottom and side faces of a submerged cuboid.

blocks.heading: The lower face wins
content: In a static fluid of uniform density, pressure increases with depth. The formula to remember is Δp = ρgΔh. Here Δp is the pressure difference between two levels, ρ is fluid density, g is gravitational field strength and Δh is their vertical separation.

The lower face is deeper than the upper face, so p_bottom is greater than p_top. If the two horizontal faces have the same area A, the upward force p_bottom A is greater than the downward force p_top A.

The difference between those two forces is upward. This upward resultant of the fluid pressure forces is called upthrust. We have explained its origin without using the displaced-volume equation that belongs to the next lesson.

symbols: Δp is hydrostatic pressure difference in pascals, Pa.
ρ is fluid density in kilograms per cubic metre, kg m⁻³.
g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram, N kg⁻¹.
Δh is vertical depth difference in metres, m.
formula_to_remember.units: Using kg m⁻³, N kg⁻¹ and m gives pressure difference in Pa.

figure.purpose: Show the causal chain from greater depth to a larger lower-face force and an upward resultant.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper comparison diagram of equal-area top and bottom faces at depths h_top and h_bottom. Show a shorter downward arrow p_top A and a longer upward arrow p_bottom A. Beside it show the subtraction p_bottom A minus p_top A as one upward resultant labelled upthrust.
figure.alt_text: The deeper bottom face has a larger upward pressure force than the downward force on the top face.

blocks.heading: What happens to the sideways pushes?
content: Consider two opposite vertical faces of a symmetric block in still water. Matching points on the two faces are at the same depth, so they have the same pressure. The areas also match, so their horizontal forces are equal and opposite.
Those horizontal forces cancel in pairs. They do not create the vertical upthrust. The vertical resultant remains because the lower surface is at greater depth than the upper surface.

The same idea works on a curved object by pairing small surface patches. Horizontal components from appropriate opposite patches cancel, while the vertical pressure-force components have an upward resultant.

figure.purpose: Make the pairwise cancellation of horizontal components visible for flat and curved surfaces.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 split teacher sketch. Left: symmetric cuboid with equal opposite horizontal arrows at matching depths crossing out as a pair. Right: rounded body with two matching side patches and resolved horizontal components cancelling. Keep a separate upward resultant arrow only as the conclusion.
figure.alt_text: Equal horizontal pressure-force components on opposite sides cancel in pairs.

blocks.heading: From depth difference to upthrust
content: A sealed rectangular sensor has horizontal top and bottom faces, each of area 0.015 m². It is fully immersed in water. The bottom face is 0.20 m deeper than the top face. Take ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.
First find the pressure difference: Δp = ρgΔh = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.20 = 1962 Pa. This is not either absolute face pressure. It is the amount by which the bottom pressure exceeds the top pressure.

Now compare forces on equal areas: upthrust = ΔF = Δp A = 1962 × 0.015 = 29.43 N, so 29 N to two significant figures. The unit check is Pa m² = N. The direction check is upward because the larger force is on the lower face.

figure.purpose: Model the complete pressure-difference to force-difference route with units and direction.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper worked layout. Left: original rectangular sensor with top and bottom separation 0.20 m and face area 0.015 m². Right: four coloured steps for Δp = ρgΔh, ΔF = ΔpA, 29 N and upward direction, including Pa m² = N as the unit check.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout converts a 0.20 metre depth difference into a 29 newton upward resultant.

blocks.heading: Pressure is not only an upward push
content: It is tempting to say that water pressure acts upward because submerged objects can feel lighter. That idea feels reasonable, but pressure itself has no single upward direction. At a surface, its force is normal to that surface.

The upward result appears only after all the pressure forces are combined. Sideways components cancel appropriately, the top contributes downward, and the deeper lower region contributes a larger upward component.

Another tempting shortcut is to say that the fluid is simply supporting the object. That names an effect but does not explain its origin. The causal explanation must mention unequal hydrostatic pressure and the resulting unequal pressure forces.

figure.purpose: Correct the claim that pressure itself acts only upward and summarise the valid causal chain.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper correction panel. Cross out one incorrect single arrow labelled pressure upward. Replace it with normal arrows around a body, paired side cancellation, larger lower contribution and a compact chain: greater depth, greater pressure, greater force, upward resultant.
figure.alt_text: Pressure acts normally around the object, and unequal forces combine to give an upward resultant.

blocks.heading: The explanation in one chain
content: Start with depth: the lower part of an immersed object is deeper, so the fluid pressure there is greater. Convert pressure to force using the area and surface direction.
Combine the forces: appropriate horizontal components cancel, while the larger lower pressure-force contribution exceeds the upper contribution. The resultant is upward and is called upthrust.
Stay inside this lesson's boundary. Use Δp = ρgΔh and F = pA when data are supplied. Do not replace the reasoning with the displaced-fluid formula or floating-equilibrium equations, which come next.

concepts_taught: Upthrust as the upward resultant of fluid pressure forces
Greater hydrostatic pressure at greater depth
Unequal top and bottom pressure forces
Pairwise cancellation of appropriate horizontal pressure-force components
misconceptions_addressed: All pressure forces around a submerged object cancel.
Naming fluid support is enough to explain the origin of upthrust.
Absolute depth is required when only a pressure difference is needed.
next_lesson_can_assume: Explain that upthrust originates from a hydrostatic pressure difference.
Relate greater lower pressure to a larger upward pressure force.
Recognise cancellation of appropriate sideways pressure-force components.
Calculate upthrust from Δp and equal face area when both are supplied or can be found.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Upthrust calculated from fluid density and displaced volume.
Upthrust set equal to weight for floating equilibrium.
Fluid flow, drag or stability theory.
